Learning Objectives

•  Define ROS as middleware and explain its modular architecture
•  Describe nodes, packages, and the ROS computational graph
•  Explain publish–subscribe communication using topics
•   Differentiate between topics, services, and parameters
•  Understand the sensor–compute–actuator workflow in robotics
•  Relate ROS concepts to real-world deployment on edge AI hardware (Jetson)
•  Interpret basic robot structure and spatial relationships
   (URDF & TF)

slides.title: What is ROS?
slides.text:
What is ROS?

•  Robot Operating System (ROS) is an open-source framework that provides tools,
    libraries, and conventions to simplify the task of creating complex and robust
   robot behavior across a wide variety of robotic platforms.

   Open Source                        Middleware
   BSD/Apache-2.0 licensed,                Abstraction layer for hardware &
   community-driven since 2007            software communication


   Ecosystem                              Cross-Platform
   1000+ packages, 10,000+ users            Linux, macOS, Windows support
   worldwide                                  in ROS 2




                                                                                                           4

Definition and four cards: open source with BSD/Apache-2.0/community wording; middleware abstraction; ecosystem counts of 1000+ packages and 10000+ users; ROS 2 support for Linux, macOS and Windows. Counts are source claims, not current measurements.

    2024  ROS 2 Jazzy — latest LTS release

slides.title: Concept of Robotic Middleware
slides.text:
Concept of Robotic Middleware

•  Despite its name, ROS is not a traditional operating
   system like Windows, macOS, or Linux.
•   It cannot run directly on computer hardware; instead, it
   requires a host operating system, typically Ubuntu Linux,
   to function.
•  ROS is best defined as middleware: a software layer that
    sits between the operating system and the robotic
   applications you write.
•  Think of ROS as the toolkit that provides functionalities
   that facilitates “communication system” to a robot.
•   Its main job is to make communication between different
   parts of a robot simple and organized.

                                                                                                           7

visualInspection.notes: Individually viewed sources/previews/lectures/page-0177.webp at 1800x1013 with extracted text. Printed 7. Four-layer figure, bottom to top: hardware; Ubuntu host OS on Jetson; ROS middleware with communication/messages/tools; application with Python AI/navigation. Body distinguishes middleware from traditional operating system.

slides.title: Concept of Robotic Middleware (Cont.)
slides.text:
Concept of Robotic Middleware (Cont.)

•   It acts as the "plumbing" of a robot, providing the underlying communication
   protocols (Inter-Process Communication or IPC) so that different programs can
    talk to one another without the developer having to write complex networking
   code from scratch.
•  The data—such as images, sensor readings, or movement commands—is like
   water. The programs are like rooms in the building. ROS provides the pipes that
   carry data between these rooms.
•  As a developer, one can use ROS tools to send and
   receive data. This abstraction is what makes ROS
   powerful and easy to scale.
•   In ROS, each function (like "Read Camera" or "Turn
   Wheels") is an independent program.

                                                                                                           8

visualInspection.notes: Individually viewed sources/previews/lectures/page-0178.webp at 1800x1013 with extracted text. Printed 8. Plumbing analogy: programs are rooms, data is water, ROS communication is pipes/IPC. Images, sensor readings and movement commands illustrate exchanged data.

slides.title: The Philosophy: Modular Open System Architecture (MOSA)
slides.text:
The Philosophy: Modular Open System Architecture (MOSA)

•  The core design philosophy of ROS is modularity through a Modular Open
   System Architecture (MOSA).
•  Imagine the electrical outlets in your home. Because they use a standardized
   interface (the plug), you can connect a lamp, a toaster, or a laptop without
   knowing how the power grid works.
•  ROS does this for robotics software:
    –  Modularity: You can develop, debug, and test a
        "Navigation" module independently from a "Speech
        Recognition" module. (python modules)
    – Code Reuse: Because interfaces are standardized, you don't
       have to "reinvent the wheel." If someone has written a
        world-class driver for a specialized 3D camera, you can
       simply plug it into your ROS system.

                                                                                                           9

visualInspection.notes: Individually viewed sources/previews/lectures/page-0179.webp at 1800x1013 with extracted text. Printed 9. MOSA uses a standardized outlet analogy. Navigation and speech modules can be developed/tested separately, and compatible drivers reused. Standardization is not a plug-anything guarantee.

slides.title: Why Use ROS for Artificial Intelligence?
slides.text:
Why Use ROS for Artificial Intelligence?

•  For AI-driven robotics, ROS is essential because it decouples perception from
   control.
•   In AI robotics, we often use heavy computational models like Convolutional
   Neural Networks (CNNs) for vision. These models process data at different
   speeds than the motors.
•  ROS allows:
    – Asynchronous Processing: Your AI module can take its time
        to "think" (process an image) while safety module
       continues to run at a high frequency to avoid obstacles.
    –  Standardized Data: AI models require specific inputs (like
        arrays of pixels). ROS provides standard Messages so your
       Python AI code can talk to hardware drivers written by
      someone else.

                                                                                                          10

visualInspection.notes: Individually viewed sources/previews/lectures/page-0180.webp at 1800x1013 with extracted text. Printed 10. Slow CNN perception is decoupled from faster control/safety processing. Standard message inputs connect AI to drivers. Essential wording does not establish that ROS is uniquely necessary.

slides.title: Hardware: The NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano
slides.text:
Hardware: The NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano

•  To run an intelligent middleware like ROS, a robot needs a centralized “brain”.
•   In this course, we use the NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano as our primary computing
   platform.
•  Role in ROS:
    –  The Jetson acts as the centralized computing host.
    –  While a simple microcontroller (like an Arduino) is excellent for moving motors, as it lacks the
       power to run the Linux-based ROS middleware or complex AI models.
•  Edge AI Capability:
    –  The Jetson is uniquely suited for ROS because it contains high-
        performance GPUs (Graphics Processing Units).
    –  In a ROS workflow, the Jetson runs the "Vision Node" using its GPU
         to accelerate AI detection, while simultaneously running the
        "Middleware" to coordinate the robot’s movement.


                                                                                                          11

visualInspection.notes: Individually viewed sources/previews/lectures/page-0181.webp at 1800x1013 with extracted text. Printed 11. The course uses a Jetson Orin Nano host for GPU-assisted vision and middleware coordination, alongside a simpler Arduino motor-control role. Centralization is the example architecture, not a universal requirement.

slides.title: Building blocks of ROS
slides.text:
Building blocks of ROS

•  For a robotic system to be “intelligent”, it must be broken down
   into manageable pieces that can run simultaneously on hardware.
   – Nodes: Individual programs in ROS that perform specific tasks
   – Topics: Communication channels through which nodes continuously
      exchange data.
   – Services: Provide request–response communication between nodes for
        specific tasks.
   – Actions: combine topics and services
   – Messages: Define the data format used for
      communication between nodes.
   – Packages: Organized collections of ROS files (nodes,
      messages, configs) used to build applications.
                                                                                                          12

visualInspection.notes: Individually viewed sources/previews/lectures/page-0182.webp at 1800x1013 with extracted text. Printed 12. Six building blocks: nodes perform tasks; topics carry continuous data; services provide request/response; actions combine communication for goals; messages define data formats; packages organize files. Final package line overlaps the footer but is readable.

slides.title: ROS Node: The Atomic Unit of Computation
slides.text:
ROS Node: The Atomic Unit of Computation

•  A Node is a single-purpose programming module or a
   process that performs computation.                       Came
                                                                                                                            Lidar             Control
                                                                                                     ra•   In a ROS-based robot, you do not write one massive                   Node           Node                                                                            Node
   program; instead, you write many small programs
   (python scripts) called nodes.
                                                                              SLAM            Nav•  These Multiple small programs (nodes) work together
                                                                                   Node            Node
   using ROS functionalities.
•  The core idea behind nodes is “divide and simplify”.
•  Features of Node:
    –  Single Responsibility: Each node should do one thing well.
       For example, one node might read images from a camera,
       while another node performs AI object detection, and a
        third node sends commands to the motor controller.


                                                                                                          13

Single-purpose computational nodes divide camera, detection and motor responsibilities. The camera/LiDAR/control and SLAM/navigation diagram has lines without arrowheads, so it does not define a directed message trace.

slides.title: ROS Node: (Cont.)
slides.text:
ROS Node: (Cont.)

   – Isolation and Reliability:
           • Because each node runs as a separate process, if “AI detection node” crashes
          due to a software bug, it does not necessarily crash the “motor control node”.
           •  This isolation is critical for robot safety.
   – Node on Hardware:
           • On Jetson Orin Nano, you can utilize the multi-core CPU and powerful GPU by
           running different nodes on different cores.
           • Offload a specific "Vision Node" to the GPU while the
           “Path Planning Node” runs on the CPU.





                                                                                                          14

visualInspection.notes: Individually viewed sources/previews/lectures/page-0184.webp at 1800x1013 with extracted text. Printed 14. Separate-process example limits direct crash propagation. GPU vision and CPU planning appear in the diagram. Process survival does not prove safe control, and one-node-one-process or automatic scheduling is not a universal invariant.

slides.title: ROS Package: Organizing Software
slides.text:
ROS Package: Organizing Software

•  A Package is the fundamental unit of software organization in ROS.
•  A package is a folder (collection) that contains everything needed for a specific
   functionality in ROS.
•    If a node is a worker, then a package is the workplace where that worker lives.
•  A package contains the node's source code, configuration files, and data files.
•  This can be understood as a custom python packages which has specific
   functionality





                                                                                                          15

visualInspection.notes: Individually viewed sources/previews/lectures/page-0185.webp at 1800x1013 with extracted text. Printed 15. A package groups source, configuration and data. Worker/workplace analogy contrasts running nodes and organizational folders; camera/detection/motor folders appear above runtime-node boxes.

slides.title: Computational Graph
slides.text:
Computational Graph

•  When all your independent nodes start running and
   communicating, they form what is known as the ROS Graph.
•  This graph is a peer-to-peer network of all the processes in the
   system.
•  On an abstract level for a AI robotics workflow, your graph
   might look like this:
     1.  Camera Node publishes raw images.
     2.   AI Detection Node (running a CNN) receives those images
        and identifies an object.
     3.   Navigation Node decides how to move toward that object.
     4.   Drive Node turns those decisions into physical wheel
        movements.


                                                                                                          16

visualInspection.notes: Individually viewed sources/previews/lectures/page-0186.webp at 1800x1013 with extracted text. Printed 16. Directed chain: Camera Node -- /camera/raw --> AI Detection -- /detected_objects --> Navigation -- /cmd_vel --> Drive. These exact names differ from the /image_raw example elsewhere.

slides.title: Conceptual Python Workflow
slides.text:
Conceptual Python Workflow

•  To create a node in Python, we use the rclpy python
    library.
•  Many other libraires that supports ROS functionalities
   are available.
•  Conceptually, the workflow is always the same:
    –  Initialize: Tell ROS that this Python script is starting up
       (rclpy.init()).
    –  Create the Node: Define a class that represents your node
       with node name “my_node”.
    –  Spin: Put the node into a loop so it stays alive to listen for
       data and process AI tasks (rclpy.spin(node)).
    – Shutdown: Cleanly exit when the robot is turned off.


                                                                                                          17

Visually read code imports rclpy and Node, declares class MyNode(Node), calls super().__init__('my_node'), and uses main with init, node construction, spin and shutdown. Screenshot code was absent from extracted text.

slides.title: ROS Topics: Asynchronous Data Streams
slides.text:
ROS Topics: Asynchronous Data Streams

•  The most common way nodes exchange information in ROS is by using Topics,
   which is based on a Publish-Subscribe paradigm.                  SUBSCRIBER
            PUBLISHER                                                                                                       Vision Node
                                                        TOPIC                                                                                                       receives /image_raw        Camera Node                                                     /image_raw                                                                                                         callback triggers          publishes /image_raw                                                   sensor_msgs/Image
          at 30 Hz
•  This is an asynchronous communication model, meaning nodes don't have to
   wait for a response to continue their work.
    –  Decoupling: Topics decouple the “transmitters" of data from the “receivers". A
       camera node just publishes images; it doesn't need to know
            if an AI node, a logging node, or a human operator is actually
       watching those images.
    – Many-to-Many: One topic can have multiple publishers
          (e.g., two different GPS sensors) and multiple subscribers
          (e.g., a map-builder and a safety-monitor) simultaneously.

                                                                                                          18

visualInspection.notes: Individually viewed sources/previews/lectures/page-0188.webp at 1800x1013 with extracted text. Printed 18. Camera publisher at 30 Hz sends sensor_msgs/Image through /image_raw to a vision subscriber/callback. Pub-sub is asynchronous and permits multiple publishers/subscribers.

slides.title: Publishers and Subscribers: The "Radio Station" Analogy
slides.text:
Publishers and Subscribers: The "Radio Station" Analogy

•  To understand topics, consider a Radio Station:
   – The Topic is the Frequency: A specific channel (e.g., 98.7 FM or in ROS,
      /camera/image_raw) where data is broadcast.
   – The Publisher is the Transmitter: The node
       that broadcasts data onto that frequency.
   – The Subscriber is the Radio Receiver:
      Any node that tunes into that specific frequency to receive the broadcast.
   – Anonymity:
             •  The transmitter doesn't know who is listening, and the listener
             doesn't need to know where the transmitter is located
             •  They only need to agree on the "frequency" (topic name) and
            the "language" (message type).


                                                                                                          19

visualInspection.notes: Individually viewed sources/previews/lectures/page-0189.webp at 1800x1013 with extracted text. Printed 19. Radio transmitter maps to publisher, frequency/channel to topic and receivers to subscribers. The 98.7 FM illustration fans out to three receivers. Agreement on topic name and message type is highlighted but is not a complete QoS/network guarantee.

slides.title: ROS Messages: Standardizing the Language
slides.text:
ROS Messages: Standardizing the Language

• Nodes must speak the same language to communicate. In ROS,
   this "language" is the Message.
   – Message Types (Interfaces): A message is a strictly defined data structure
         (e.g., an integer, a string, or a complex array of pixels).
   – Common AI Messages:
             • sensor_msgs/Image: Used for raw camera data.
             • geometry_msgs/Twist: Used for movement commands (Linear and Angular velocity).
   – Jetson handles high-bandwidth messages, like 4K
       video streams, using optimized ROS message
       structures that minimize the "cost" of moving data
      between AI nodes and hardware drivers.



                                                                                                          20

visualInspection.notes: Individually viewed sources/previews/lectures/page-0190.webp at 1800x1013 with extracted text. Printed 20. Messages are structured interfaces. sensor_msgs/Image carries raw camera data; geometry_msgs/Twist expresses linear/angular velocities. The 4K-transfer discussion gives no measured throughput or zero-copy guarantee.

slides.title: Conceptual Python Workflow
slides.text:
Conceptual Python Workflow

•  When writing a Python node to use topics, the logic follows the same pattern as
    in the nodes
•  Now the additional functionalities of topic is introduced in our custom class
   with a specific pattern:
    –  For a Publisher: create_timer() → calls publish_msg() repeatedly
             •  Create Publisher using create_publisher()
             •  Create a "timer" that calls a function at a set frequency (e.g., 10Hz) to broadcast data.
    –  For a Subscriber: create_subscription()→ triggers callback()
               •  Create Subscriber using create_subscription()
             •  Register a Call back Function callback(msg)
             •  Callback function is a piece of code that sits idle until a new
           message arrives on the topic, at which point it "wakes up" to
             process the data.

                                                                                                          21

visualInspection.notes: Individually viewed sources/previews/lectures/page-0191.webp at 1800x1013 with extracted text. Printed 21. Publisher uses create_publisher and create_timer to invoke publish_msg; subscriber uses create_subscription and callback(msg) on message arrival. Timer and subscription triggers differ.

slides.title: ROS Services
slides.text:
ROS Services

•  While Topics are ideal for continuous data like sensor streams, robots often
   need to perform specific tasks "on demand" or adjust their settings without
   restarting their software.
•  A service is a communication method where one node sends a request, and
   another node sends back a response.
•  This is a synchronous communication model based on a Client-Server
   relationship.
•  Services are used when:
    – You need a guaranteed response
    – You are performing a specific task
    – You cannot continue without the result



                                                                                                          23

visualInspection.notes: Individually viewed sources/previews/lectures/page-0193.webp at 1800x1013 with extracted text. Printed 23. Services use on-demand client/server request-response rather than continuous streams. Guaranteed-response and universally synchronous wording is overbroad; printed slide 29 explicitly uses call_async.

slides.title: ROS Services (Cont.)
slides.text:
ROS Services (Cont.)

•  Unlike a radio broadcast (Topic), a service is like a phone call.
    – A Client (the caller) sends a specific Request to a Server (the receiver).
    – The Server processes the request and sends back a Response (the answer).
•  Synchronicity: In a service call, the client node typically waits for the server to
    finish its work and reply before moving on to the next step in its program.
•  One-to-Many (One Server): In ROS, while many different
   nodes can act as Clients and call the same service, there
   can only be one Server providing that specific service at
   any time.
•  Eg: AI navigation node might use a service to "Reset the
  Map" or "Trigger a Snapshot" from a 3D camera,.



                                                                                                          24

visualInspection.notes: Individually viewed sources/previews/lectures/page-0194.webp at 1800x1013 with extracted text. Printed 24. slides.title: Actions: Long-Running Tasks
slides.text:
Actions: Long-Running Tasks
 Actions combine topics and services for preemptable, goal-oriented tasks with
 continuous feedback. Ideal for navigation, manipulation, and multi-step processes.



      Goal             Accepted           Feedback              Result              Cancel


                                 Server publishes Final response
  Client sends     Server accepts                                         Client can cancel
                                       periodic       when
 goal to server    or rejects goal                                     anytime
                                  updates       complete
 Actions use three topics internally: goal, feedback, and result. The
 .action file defines the interfaces for all three.
 Example: /navigate_to_pose (Nav2) — sends goal pose, receives
 progress, delivers final result





                                                                                                          26

visualInspection.notes: Individually viewed sources/previews/lectures/page-0196.webp at 1800x1013 with extracted text. Printed 26. Action diagram includes goal, accepted, feedback, result and cancel; text allows acceptance/rejection and uses navigate_to_pose. Cancellation capability does not imply unconditional success after completion. The three-topics-internally statement remains flagged rather than treated as a complete ROS 2 transport inventory.

slides.title: ROS Parameters
slides.text:
ROS Parameters

•  Robotic environments change constantly. You shouldn't have to rewrite and
   recompile your Python code just to change a camera's resolution or an AI
   model's sensitivity.
•  Parameters allow you to configure a node's settings at runtime.
    –  Parameters are essentially configuration variables (like a string, integer, or boolean) that "live"
         inside a node.
    –  Dynamic Adjustments: You can change parameters while the robot is running.

•  For example, if your AI vision node is struggling with low
    light on the NVIDIA Jetson, you can increase the
   "exposure" or "brightness" parameter through a terminal
  command without stopping the running node.




                                                                                                          27

visualInspection.notes: Individually viewed sources/previews/lectures/page-0197.webp at 1800x1013 with extracted text. Printed 27. Node-local named configuration values include string/integer/boolean examples and runtime exposure/brightness adjustments. Runtime effects require supported updates consumed by active logic.

slides.title: Conceptual Python Workflow
slides.text:
Conceptual Python Workflow

• When implementing logic in Python, the workflow is streamlined
   to focus on the interaction:
   – For Services:
           • Define a Service Name and an Interface (the structure of the request and
            response).
           • The client script will typically use a "Wait for Service" function to ensure the
            Jetson has the server online before attempting to send a command.
   – For Parameters:
           •  In Python node's constructor (__init__), declare the
           parameters needed and set their default values.
           • Throughout AI logic, "get" the current value of that
           parameter to decide how the robot should behave.


                                                                                                          28

visualInspection.notes: Individually viewed sources/previews/lectures/page-0198.webp at 1800x1013 with extracted text. Printed 28. Services use a name and request-response interface with availability checking. Parameters are declared with defaults in construction and read later. Availability is distinct from a completed result.

slides.title: Sensor–Compute–Actuator Loop
slides.text:
Sensor–Compute–Actuator Loop

•  Deploying ROS on Jetson hardware facilitates a continuous cycle of data flow
   that allows the robot to interact with its environment autonomously.
•  Complete Cycle involves:
    –  Input - Sensing:
           • High-end sensors like 3D depth cameras or LiDAR interface directly with the
            Jetson via USB or CSI ports, publishing raw data to ROS topics.
    – Computation:
           • ROS nodes running on the Jetson subscribe to these
           sensor topics.
           •  Eg. The "Vision Node" might use the GPU to detect an
             object, while a "Decision Node" determines the next
         movement based on AI logic.


                                                                                                          30

visualInspection.notes: Individually viewed sources/previews/lectures/page-0200.webp at 1800x1013 with extracted text. Printed 30. Depth camera/LiDAR input, with USB/CSI examples, is published through sensor drivers. GPU perception subscribes and detects; decision logic selects movement. Connection examples are not universal for every sensor.

slides.weekMappingEvidence: Course outline, lectures PDF physical page 3; chronological lecture-title grouping matches outline topics. Visual confirmation tracked in lecture_map.json.

slides.title: Sensor–Compute–Actuator Loop (Cont.)
slides.text:
Sensor–Compute–Actuator Loop (Cont.)

   – Output - Actuation:
             •  The Jetson sends refined commands (often via serial communication) to a low-level
              microcontroller, such as an Arduino, which handles the precise timing of Pulse Width
            Modulation (PWM) to move the motors.





                                                                                                          31

visualInspection.notes: Individually viewed sources/previews/lectures/page-0201.webp at 1800x1013 with extracted text. Printed 31. Chain: 3D camera; sensor_msgs/Image; Jetson ROS/Python AI/GPU; serial-data/PWM label; Arduino/motor shield; H-bridge; DC motors; physical motion. Body assigns precise PWM timing to the low-level microcontroller, not to CNN inference.

slides.title: URDF and Transforms (TF)
slides.text:
URDF and Transforms (TF)

•  Unified Robot Description Format (URDF) provides a mathematical description
   of the robot's physical body.
•  Definition: A URDF is an XML-based file that describes the visual appearance,
   physical dimensions, and kinematic structure of a robot.
•  URDF comprises
    –  Links: Represent the rigid parts of the robot (e.g., the chassis, a camera mount, or a wheel).
               •  Each link can have a Visual property (what we see in RViz),
             a Collision property (used by Gazebo to prevent the robot from "ghosting" through walls),
             an Inertial property (mass and balance for physics simulation).
    –  Joints:
               •  These define the relationship between two links.
               •  They specify where the links are connected and how they move (e.g.,
               Fixed for a camera, Continuous for a wheel, or Revolute for a robotic
            arm hinge).


                                                                                                          32

visualInspection.notes: Individually viewed sources/previews/lectures/page-0202.webp at 1800x1013 with extracted text. Printed 32. URDF is XML for appearance, dimensions and kinematic structure. Rigid links have visual, collision and inertial properties. Joint examples are fixed camera mount, continuous wheel and revolute arm hinge. A model property alone is not a safety certificate.

slides.title: Transforms (TF): Tracking the Robot in 3D Space
slides.text:
Transforms (TF): Tracking the Robot in 3D Space

•  A TF (Transform) is the mathematical relationship between two coordinate
   frames in 3D space.
•  While URDF is the static blueprint, Transforms are the live, mathematical
   calculations of where each part is located at any time.
•  TF Tree:
    –  TFs are organized into a hierarchical tree. Every link has one Parent and can have multiple
         Children.
    –  For example, the base_link (chassis) is often the parent of the camera_link. If the robot moves,
        the entire tree updates accordingly.
•  Asynchronous Distribution:
    –  ROS publishes these spatial relationships on a dedicated topic (/tf).
    –  Any node on the Jetson (say object detector)—can subscribe to this
         topic to find out exactly where a sensor is located at any time.


                                                                                                          33

visualInspection.notes: Individually viewed sources/previews/lectures/page-0203.webp at 1800x1013 with extracted text. Printed 33. TF represents mathematical relations between coordinate frames in 3D. The tree example places camera_link below base_link; non-root frames have one parent and may have children. URDF is the blueprint, while TF supplies changing frame relations. The /tf topic distributes transforms. Exactness and availability require valid, timely transforms, not merely subscription.

slides.printedNumberEvidence: Extracted from actual bottom-right footer region; not inferred from physical page.
slides.weekMappingEvidence: Course outline, lectures PDF physical page 3; chronological lecture-title grouping matches outline topics. Visual confirmation tracked in lecture_map.json.

slides.title: How URDF Generates TF?
slides.text:
How URDF Generates TF?

•  The bridge between the static URDF file and
   the dynamic TF system is a core ROS node
   called the robot_state_publisher.
    –  Input 1 (URDF): The node reads the robot_description
        parameter to understand the robot's structure.
    –  Input 2 (Joint States): It listens to the /joint_states
          topic, which provides the current angles of the
        motors (e.g., "The arm is currently at 45 degrees").
    –  Processing: It performs the mathematical
        calculations (forward kinematics) to determine
       the 3D position of every link
    –  Output (TF): It publishes the final 3D coordinates for
        every part of the robot to the /tf topic, thus
        generating simulated results.

                                                                                                          34

visualInspection.notes: Individually viewed sources/previews/lectures/page-0204.webp at 1800x1013 with extracted text. Printed 34. robot_state_publisher takes robot_description (URDF structure) and /joint_states (current joint positions), applies forward kinematics, and publishes frame transforms. The diagram labels /tf as a live 3D map; this is not an occupancy map or a physics simulation. The slide omits the fixed-transform /tf_static distinction, so questions avoid treating all transforms as dynamic /tf messages.

slides.title: Bridging Simulation and Real Deployment
slides.text:
Bridging Simulation and Real Deployment

•  One of the greatest advantages of the ROS framework on Jetson hardware is
   the ability to move from Simulation to Real-World Deployment with minimal
   code changes.
    –  Digital Twins:
           • Developers often use Gazebo to simulate the robot's physical properties
              (gravity, friction) and RViz to visualize.
    – Hardware Abstraction:
           • ROS decouples the computation logic from the
          hardware drivers.
           •  So, Python-based navigation node doesn't know if it is
             talking to a simulated motor in Gazebo or a real motor
             controller on the Jetson.



                                                                                                          35

visualInspection.notes: Individually viewed sources/previews/lectures/page-0205.webp at 1800x1013 with extracted text. Printed 35. Sim-to-real uses middleware abstraction and common interfaces to reuse robot computation. Gazebo supplies simulated physical effects; RViz visualizes robot data. Minimal code changes is a design aim, not proof of identical real-world behavior.

slides.printedNumberEvidence: Extracted from actual bottom-right footer region; not inferred from physical page.
slides.weekMappingEvidence: Course outline, lectures PDF physical page 3; chronological lecture-title grouping matches outline topics. Visual confirmation tracked in lecture_map.json.

slides.title: Bridging Simulation and Real Deployment (Cont.)
slides.text:
Bridging Simulation and Real Deployment (Cont.)

   – The Bridge:
           • During deployment, you simply swap the Simulation Bridge for a Hardware
            Driver node.
           • The communication topics (like /cmd_vel) remain identical, ensuring that the
           behavior tested in simulation transfers accurately to the Jetson Orin Nano.





                                                                                                          36

visualInspection.notes: Individually viewed sources/previews/lectures/page-0206.webp at 1800x1013 with extracted text. Printed 36. Replace a Simulation Bridge with a Hardware Driver while keeping interfaces such as /cmd_vel stable. The diagram contrasts Gazebo/RViz and a Jetson robot. Interface reuse does not guarantee matching friction, noise, delay, or dynamics.

slides.title: Summary
slides.text:
Summary

•  A robot is made of many small programs working together
•  ROS helps these programs communicate and work as one system
•  Different methods (topics, services, parameters) control how data is shared
•  Jetson allows the robot to run AI and make decisions in real time
•  Robots follow a loop: sense → think → act
•  URDF and TF help the robot understand its body and position in space





                                                                                                          39

visualInspection.notes: Individually viewed sources/previews/lectures/page-0209.webp at 1800x1013 with extracted text. Printed 39. Summary connects small cooperating programs, topics/services/parameters, Jetson AI processing, the sense-think-act loop, and URDF/TF body-space representation. No numerical timing or unconditional real-time guarantee is provided.
